name: Western Desert Language, Warburton Ranges dialect
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Douglas, W. H. 1958 [inner title page dated 1957]. An Introduction to the Western Desert Language of Australia: a pedagogical description of the Western Desert language, based on the dialect spoken at Warburton Ranges, Western Australia. Oceania Linguistic Monographs 4 (eds A. Capell & S. Wurm). Sydney: University of Sydney. Part One 'Pronunciation' (Rosetta Project extract 'Ngaanyatjarra Phonology', 8 pp., archive.org).
catalog_locator: Part One 'Pronunciation', Section 3 'Stress or Accent', A 'Syllable Stress', p. 8; restated in 'Summary of Pronunciation', C 'Rules', p. 16.
catalog_quote: SECTION 3. STRESS OR ACCENT. A. SYLLABLE STRESS. The FIRST syllable of each word is stressed (or accented). E.g. kutjara 'two' is pronounced kú - tjara. In words of more than three syllables the primary stress is still on the first syllable, but a secondary stress generally falls on the third syllable. E.g. yulparira 'south' is pronounced "yulpa-'rira. In certain compounds, where this rule does not apply, a hyphen is inserted. Each part of the compound then takes stress on the first syllable. E.g. kutjara-kutjara 'four. B. SENTENCE STRESS. Sentence stress is heavier (or louder) than syllable stress and occurs on items the speaker wishes to emphasise within sentences. [p. 8] ... C. RULES. ... STRESS: Primary syllable stress always occurs on first syllable of the word. [p. 16]
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress is fixed on the initial syllable of every word; in words longer than three syllables a secondary stress usually falls on the third syllable; in (hyphenated) reduplicative/compound words each member carries its own initial stress. No reference to vowel length or syllable weight in stress placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'a secondary stress generally falls on the third syllable' in words of more than three syllables (example ˌ/ˈ marks: "yulpa-'rira for yulparira 'south'); nothing said about further alternating stresses in longer words.
new_statements.exceptions: Certain compounds (written with a hyphen) where each part takes initial stress, e.g. kutjara-kutjara 'four'; sentence stress (emphatic items, interrogative particles) is heavier than syllable stress and is described separately (Section 3B).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule for citation/word forms in a pedagogical description of the Warburton Ranges dialect; sentence stress and intonation contours are treated as separate phrase-level phenomena (Sections 3B, 4).
new_statements.identity_note: Douglas 1958 is titled 'Western Desert Language' (and StressTyp/WALS file both Douglas and Glass & Hackett 1970 under 'Pitjantjatjara', WALS code pit), but the title page states the description is 'based on the dialect spoken at Warburton Ranges, Western Australia', i.e. Ngaanyatjarra proper (ngaa1240); the Rosetta Project independently tags the extract iso ntj. Not to be confused with Pitjantjatjara (pitj1243) or Ngaatjatjarra (ngaa1239-type neighbouring dialect).

sources.quote: Only languages with a documented description of fixed and word initial lexical stress are considered here, for consistency in comparing phonetic cues. (p. 4) ... This is coded as a binary (0/1) factor where the first syllable of each word is coded as 1. Words were orthographic words (p. 9) ... In four languages—Bardi, Malak Malak, Ngaanyatjarra, and Yidiny—the model predicts that stressed vowels will be around 20% longer on average (p. 12) ... in Ngaanyatjarra there are lengthening effects in glides and oral stops but not nasals. (p. 14) ... Only two languages, Ngaanyatjarra and Kayardild, had significant lengthening effects in consonants following a stressed vowel in all three consonant categories (p. 14) ... Table 3: Ngaanyatjarra — Intensity yes; F0 maximum yes; F0 range no; Vowel duration yes; Onset duration glides stops; Post-tonic duration all; Vowel space no (p. 18)
